# D-ID's Presentation Mode Turns Slides Into Interactive AI Talks

> **In short:** D-ID's Presentation Mode turns a slide deck (PDF, PowerPoint, or Google Slides) into a live, AI-led talk. Viewers can interrupt with questions, get answers on the spot, and the presentation picks up where it left off — no script required.

A few years ago, sending a deck to someone meant hoping they actually read it. Today, you can send them a deck that talks them through it and answers their questions while it goes. D-ID says its new Presentation Mode does exactly that.

## What Presentation Mode actually does

The feature is part of D-ID's agent platform. A D-ID Agent is the company's term for an AI avatar — a realistic on-screen face and voice that can present, converse, and react. With Presentation Mode, you feed that agent a slide deck: a PDF, a PowerPoint file, or a Google Slides link, according to D-ID's announcement.

Once the deck is uploaded, the agent walks the viewer through it slide by slide. Here's the part D-ID emphasizes: viewers don't have to wait until the end to ask things. They can interrupt at any moment, ask a question out loud or in text, get an answer, and the agent then resumes from wherever it was on the slide.

There's no script. You don't write what the avatar says for each slide. The agent reads the slide content and generates the narration itself, then handles questions in the same voice.

## Why this is different from a regular slide deck

Three things make this stand out from a normal PDF or slideshow:

- **The deck talks.** Instead of silent slides, you get a face and a voice guiding the viewer through each point.
- **It's two-way.** A normal presentation flows one way — speaker to audience. This one pauses and waits for questions.
- **It resumes.** When the question is answered, the agent goes back to the next slide, not the start of the deck.

## What this means for you

- **If you train or teach:** You can send one deck to a whole class or onboarding group and let each person ask their own questions at their own pace. No need to repeat yourself three times a week.
- **If you sell or pitch:** Prospects can interrupt with "wait, how does that work?" and get a real answer without booking a follow-up call.
- **If you share reports at work:** A long internal deck becomes something a colleague can actually sit with and ask questions about, instead of skim-reading at 11 p.m.
- **If you study or learn from recordings:** Anyone who's watched a recorded lecture and wished they could raise their hand will recognize what this is solving.
- **If you already use it:** Try it on a low-stakes deck first — a short product overview or training you give often — to see how the agent handles the questions you usually get.

## Wrap-up

Presentation Mode is a small shift in what a "slide deck" means — from a static file you send to something closer to a conversation you have. If you give talks for a living, train people, or send the same deck to many people who always ask the same questions, this is the kind of tool that could quietly save you hours. The next step: try it on one deck you're comfortable with and see how the agent handles the questions you usually get asked.
